claims.text: Oxidation resistance and overall material integrity in high-temperature multiprincipal-element alloys are controlled by selective surface segregation of protective elements.
Cr, Ta, and Al are low-diffusivity, high oxygen-affinity elements in the relevant alloys.
Surface enrichment of Cr, Ta, or Al produces a continuous protective Cr2O3- or CrTaO4-based scale that impedes oxygen ingress.
Higher Mn concentrations promote non-protective oxidation and accelerated degradation.
Mn-derived oxides are volatile or porous and consequently undermine scale adhesion.
The baseline alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution with a balanced distribution of protective and less-protective elements.
Reducing Mn while increasing Cr, Ta, and Al should shift the oxide scale from porous and non-protective to dense and adherent.
Isothermal oxidation in air over 800–1100 °C and 50–200 hours is the proposed test regime.
The continuity, density, and adherence of the oxide scale mediate oxidation resistance.
Differences in elemental diffusivity cause Cr, Ta, and Al to enrich at the surface during high-temperature exposure.
Protective-element enrichment generates a coherent, slow-growing, low-permeability oxide scale.
Rapid Mn diffusion and formation of volatile or non-adherent Mn oxides cause breakaway oxidation and scale spallation.
Competition between protective-scale formation and Mn-driven non-protective oxidation determines oxidation kinetics and structural integrity.
Increasing protective-element concentrations will lower oxidation mass gain, reduce oxide thickness, improve scale continuity, and improve retention of mechanical properties relative to the baseline.
A CrMnFeCoNi-type baseline exhibits oxidation dominated by non-protective Mn oxides during high-temperature air exposure.
The proposed mechanism should hold from 800 °C to 1100 °C because surface-diffusion dynamics dominate in that range.
At temperatures substantially outside 800–1100 °C, other degradation or phase-transformation mechanisms may prevail.
Failure of the modified alloys to show statistically significant improvements in mass gain, scale quality, and mechanical-property retention relative to the baseline would falsify the mechanism.
